Its available form is a name connected with a person mentioned in 1 Chronicles. Within the Hebrew corpus, it occurs twice, both occurrences belonging to 1 Chronicles 4:20. The present lexical information does not provide a separate ordinary-word definition or an English rendering, so its clearest meaning is its identifying function as a person’s name.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “greatness.” It is a noun that names greatness as a quality or condition rather than an action. In the Old Testament, it appears 13 times, describing greatness as something spoken of, recognized, or displayed. Its use includes statements about God’s greatness and the greatness associated with royal honor. The word’s normal sense remains focused on the quality of being great, while the surrounding sentence shows whose greatness is being discussed or how it is expressed.

This Hebrew word refers to “captivity”—the condition of people who have been taken from their homeland or held under another power. It is a noun describing that state rather than the act of capturing someone. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, in Ezra and Daniel, and each recorded rendering is “captivity.” Its precise emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the condition of being captive.

“Alas” is an exclamation that expresses a troubled or distressed response. It does not name a person, object, or action; instead, it gives voice to an immediate reaction. In Hebrew Old Testament usage, it appears 15 times, with “Alas” as its dominant English rendering. The precise cause of the cry comes from each verse, but the word itself marks an expressed reaction of distress. It functions as a brief spoken cry rather than a description or command.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “rain,” the water that falls from the heavens. It is used for ordinary rainfall, including rain that brings blessing to the land and rain whose absence produces drought. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 35 times, showing a consistent reference to rainfall rather than a broad range of unrelated meanings. Its use is especially clear in passages that speak of God giving rain, rain beginning after a dry period, or rain falling upon the earth.

e.t: Delaiah is a personal name, referring to individuals identified by that name rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs seven times across seven verses, with “Delaiah” as its dominant English rendering. The occurrences identify people in different Old Testament passages. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on which person named Delaiah is being discussed and on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to crystal, a clear, hard, glasslike material. It is a material term rather than an action or description of a person. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Job 28:17, so its ordinary meaning is known from a single biblical use. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but “crystal” provides the clearest supported sense.

This Hebrew word means “loved.” It functions as a verbal description, presenting someone as the object of love rather than naming a person, place, or thing. Its recorded use is limited to one occurrence in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at Deuteronomy 33:3. Because the available wording is brief and the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence depends on its immediate context. Its basic sense remains a description of someone as loved.

This Hebrew word refers to a thin, flexible strand used as a “line” or “thread.” It can describe something used for fastening, measuring, marking, or making a physical connection. In the Old Testament, it occurs seven times, including descriptions of Rahab’s identifying cord, Delilah’s binding material, and the slender metal pieces associated with temple construction. Its precise function depends on the object and surrounding sentence, but the ordinary idea remains a narrow strand serving a practical purpose.

This Hebrew verb describes something becoming “changed” or going “away.” It can express a person or thing shifting from one state or place to another, so its precise sense depends on the sentence in which it appears. The word occurs 28 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including uses rendered “changed” and “away.” It functions as an action word rather than naming a person, place, or object.

This Hebrew word refers to a “division,” identifying something arranged or recognized as separate. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, so its normal meaning is represented by a single biblical occurrence rather than a broad range of uses. The word appears in 2 Chronicles 35:5; without the verse text, its precise role in that sentence cannot be described further. Its basic sense remains a division or distinct arrangement within the passage.

This Hebrew word refers to a place named “Enan” or “Hazar.” It functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. The name appears six times in the Old Testament, in three verses: twice in Numbers 34 and once in Ezekiel 48. These occurrences place it within descriptions of Israel’s boundaries and tribal territory, so its normal role is identifying a geographic location. The precise location or significance belongs to the surrounding passage, not to the name by itself.

The word occurs 12 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Ezekiel. Because the same name appears in different passages, the surrounding verse determines the referent; the lexical sense itself remains the name “Haran.”

e.t: This Hebrew word marks a position as “by,” identifying something located alongside or near a place. It is used twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Judges 9:37 and Ezekiel 38:12. In both passages, it functions as a positional term connected with a place or its central area. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its ordinary role is to indicate location in relation to something else.

This Hebrew word means to “afflict,” describing the act of bringing suffering or hardship upon someone. It is used as a verb, showing what one person or circumstance does to another. In the Old Testament, it is also rendered “afflicted,” emphasizing the person who receives this treatment. The word occurs eight times, including passages in Job, Isaiah, Lamentations, and Zephaniah, where it consistently concerns people undergoing affliction.

This Hebrew word refers to “amethyst,” a gemstone named in the Old Testament. It functions as a noun for a particular precious stone, rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Exodus: once in the description of the priestly breastpiece and again in its construction record. These occurrences identify the stone as one of the designated stones associated with that breastpiece.

This Hebrew word is a personal name, rendered “Iddo.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both times in 2 Chronicles 9:29. Its role there is tied to written records: Iddo is named among the sources consulted for information about Solomon’s acts. Since the word functions as a proper name, its meaning for a reader is chiefly identification—the particular person called Iddo—not a descriptive title or ordinary vocabulary term.

This Hebrew word means “green.” It is an adjective that describes something by its green color or condition. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Job 39:8. The word’s basic sense is therefore a color description rather than an action, person, or place. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and context, but its ordinary lexical meaning is the simple description “green.”

e.t: This Hebrew word means “little,” marking something as limited in size, amount, or extent. It appears three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, where it functions as a concise expression of smallness or a short measure. Its uses occur in passages involving birth, death, and speech, so the surrounding sentence determines precisely what is described as little. The word itself consistently points to something restricted rather than large or extensive.

e.h: A Hebrew Word for So or Thus
e.t: This Hebrew word means “so” or “thus,” pointing to the manner, result, or form of something just stated or about to be stated. It functions as a linking word, helping express that something happens in this way or follows accordingly. The word appears 37 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Exodus through Hosea. Its use can connect an instruction, action, statement, or outcome with the wording that explains how it occurs. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is “so” or “thus.”

This Hebrew verb means “make.” It describes an action performed by a person and functions as the main action word in its sentence. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Exodus 12:4, so its normal lexical meaning is supported by a single recorded use. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and the action being described there.

This word refers to the Levites, a named group mentioned in the book of Ezra. It designates them as a distinct people within the passages where it appears, rather than describing an action or quality. In this Hebrew corpus, the word occurs four times, all in Ezra. Its central meaning is therefore the group name Levites; the surrounding verse supplies the specific role or situation being discussed.

This Hebrew word means “oppressed.” It describes people being subjected to harsh pressure, control, or mistreatment. In the Old Testament, it is used as a verb describing what one person, group, or power does to others, rather than as a name for the suffering itself. The word occurs 19 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with “oppressed” as its dominant rendering. Its use includes oppression of vulnerable people and oppression carried out by foreign powers.

In English, its role may be represented by a noun or by a phrase shaped by the surrounding sentence. The precise wording can therefore vary with context, but its ordinary sense centers on what is planted. Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Micah contain its recorded occurrences.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “work.” It is a noun that names activity carried out by people, including work connected with making, building, or serving. In the Old Testament, it can be spoken of as something commanded, completed, given, or entrusted, so its sense covers purposeful activity rather than one narrow occupation. It occurs 167 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing broad use for human work and tasks, including work associated with worship and construction.

This Hebrew word means “from,” marking separation or movement away from a person, place, or thing. It functions in a sentence to show what someone or something is apart from or kept away from. The word appears 29 times in the Old Testament, so its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence. Its recorded uses span Genesis through Amos, showing that it serves this ordinary relational function across many kinds of statements.

Elihoreph is a Hebrew personal name, not a common word describing an object, action, or quality. It appears only once in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, at 1 Kings 4:3. The available rendering identifies the name as “Elihoreph,” but no supported lexical definition is provided, so its personal-name function is clearer than any proposed underlying meaning. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being named.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “commandments”: instructions or requirements given for people to obey. It functions as a noun, referring to what God commands and what people are expected to keep or do. In the Old Testament, it commonly belongs to the language of faithful obedience and is repeatedly connected with God’s commands, laws, and the duty to observe them. It occurs 184 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that this is a broad and important term for God’s revealed requirements.

This Hebrew word means “its,” marking something as belonging to or associated with something already mentioned. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Leviticus 1:16. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, the exact thing being identified must be learned from that passage; the word itself contributes the possessive relationship rather than naming the object. Its single occurrence makes it a specialized, context-dependent word rather than a broadly repeated vocabulary term.

The word means “mischief,” naming a harmful or troublesome purpose or action. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Daniel 11:27, so its broader range of use cannot be established from repeated biblical examples. The English rendering is consistent in the two recorded alignments, supporting “mischief” as the clearest ordinary meaning here. Its precise force in Daniel depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: Abishag is a personal name, referring to a woman mentioned in the account of David’s final days and Solomon’s early reign. It is not presented as a general Hebrew noun or verb with a stated definition; rather, it identifies the same individual throughout its five occurrences in the Hebrew Old Testament. The name appears in 1 Kings 1–2, where other people speak about her and she is treated as the object of actions involving the king and requests for giving. Its meaning as a personal name is therefore best kept distinct from the role she occupies in those passages.

The word refers to Mattanah, a named location mentioned in Israel’s journey. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Numbers 21:18–19. As a name, it identifies the place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In one aligned rendering, it appears with the article “the,” showing that the word can function within a larger phrase naming this location. Its precise role in each verse depends on the surrounding wording.

e.t: “Nob” is the name of a place in the Old Testament, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. It functions as a proper name for a location mentioned in connection with events in 1 Samuel, and it is also named in Nehemiah and Isaiah. The name occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with four occurrences in 1 Samuel. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding verse and its setting.

This Hebrew word means “pour.” It functions as an action word, presenting liquid as being released from one place so that it spreads or runs elsewhere. It focuses on what happens to the liquid, rather than simply naming the liquid itself. Its ten Old Testament occurrences show this action in varied statements, including images of liquid being poured out. The precise force in an individual verse depends on its surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains the act of pouring.

This Hebrew verb expresses movement upward: “ascend” or “up.” It describes going from a lower place to a higher one and functions as an action word in a sentence. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Psalm 139:8. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage, but its basic meaning is upward movement or rising.

This Hebrew word means “Folly,” referring to a state or expression of folly rather than naming a person or place. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ecclesiastes 10:6. Because no verse text or surrounding context is available here, the word’s precise force in that passage cannot be described beyond this basic lexical sense. Its use should therefore be read with the sentence around it.

This Hebrew word is the personal name “Ephai.” It functions as a name rather than a general description or action. In the Hebrew Bible, it occurs twice, both times in Jeremiah 40:8, so its meaning is chiefly its identification of a particular person. The surrounding passage is needed to explain that person’s role in the verse; the word itself does not express a broader quality, command, or idea.

This Hebrew word describes a person who is “naked,” meaning without clothing or exposed. It is used ten times in the Old Testament, including several occurrences in Genesis 3 and Ezekiel, where the condition of being unclothed is named plainly. The word functions as a straightforward description of bodily exposure rather than as a name or action. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains clear: being naked.

This Hebrew verb means “compel”: it describes causing someone to act through force, pressure, or authority rather than simple invitation. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Esther 1:8. As a verb, it expresses the action of making another person comply. The word’s basic sense is therefore active and directive, focusing on the one who imposes the requirement and the person expected to follow it.

This Hebrew word can describe something “ancient” or something “drawn,” with the surrounding sentence determining which sense fits. It is rare, occurring only twice in the Hebrew Old Testament: once in 1 Chronicles 4:22 and once in Isaiah 28:9. Because the two occurrences are rendered differently, the word should not be reduced to only one English expression. Its basic meaning is therefore context-sensitive between these two recorded senses.

Peullethai is a Hebrew personal name, rendered “Peullethai” in the available English translation. It is not presented here with an explicit definition or ordinary descriptive meaning, so it should be understood as identifying a person rather than describing an idea, action, or quality. This name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 26:5. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text and passage context.

This Hebrew noun means “rivers,” referring to substantial courses of flowing water. It is used for bodies of water in the Old Testament, including waterways associated with thirst, landscape, and the movement or force of water. The word occurs 19 times in the Hebrew Bible, so its central sense is established across multiple passages rather than being limited to one setting. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “copy,” referring to a written duplicate or document. It functions as a noun, naming the copy itself rather than describing the act of copying. The word occurs three times in the Old Testament, all in Ezra. In each occurrence, it identifies a copy, while the surrounding verse determines which document is meant. Its basic sense remains focused on a reproduced written item rather than the original.

This Hebrew word means “joined.” It describes a person or thing as connected with another, functioning as a descriptive expression rather than naming a separate object. Its five Old Testament occurrences use this central idea in contexts involving people and physical objects. The word appears in Numbers, 2 Samuel, and Psalms, showing that its basic sense remains consistent across these passages.

This Hebrew word is rendered “Shahar,” so its clearest supported sense is the name Shahar rather than a general descriptive term. It functions as a named designation in the Hebrew Old Testament data. The word occurs twice, both occurrences appearing in the same verse, Joshua 13:19. Without the surrounding verse text, no more specific contextual meaning can be stated responsibly.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to an assembled group of people—a gathered assembly or congregation. It can describe the people gathered as a body, especially in contexts involving Israel’s collective hearing, worship, decisions, or response. English Bibles commonly render it as “assembly” or “congregation,” showing that the central idea is not merely a crowd, but people gathered together. It occurs 123 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Micah. Its precise emphasis in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word refers to “disgrace,” naming a condition of dishonor. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Habakkuk 2:16, so its normal meaning is represented by a single occurrence rather than a broad range of passages. In that sentence, the word functions as the object of actions directed toward it, presenting disgrace as something brought upon or experienced by a person. The surrounding verse determines its full force there.

This Hebrew word means “soaked.” It describes something that has been saturated or prepared in a soaked condition, functioning as a descriptive word rather than naming a person or object. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Leviticus and 1 Chronicles. Its uses are connected with descriptions of preparation, so the surrounding passage determines exactly what has been soaked. The word appears in Leviticus 6:21, Leviticus 7:12, and 1 Chronicles 23:29.

e.t: “Araunah” is a personal name, referring to the individual identified by this Hebrew word. It appears eleven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all within seven verses of 2 Samuel 24. The name is consistently rendered “Araunah” in the available English renderings. Its surrounding scriptural connections place it in spoken interactions and acts of giving, but the word itself functions primarily as a person’s name rather than a description or action.

e.t: “Cry” is the central meaning of this Hebrew noun. It functions as a noun, naming what is cried out rather than describing the person who cries. The word occurs 33 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Psalms and Isaiah. It may refer to a cry expressed in speech or directed toward God, while the surrounding verse determines its particular force and significance.

This Hebrew word is a rare term whose precise ordinary meaning cannot be established from the available lexical information. It occurs three times, all in Daniel 5:2, 5:3, and 5:23, so its use is confined to that chapter within the Hebrew Old Testament record. The references identify where the word appears, but without verse text or an explicit definition, they do not establish whether it names a person, role, or object. Its exact sense therefore requires the surrounding wording of those verses.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to the stone “onyx.” It functions as a noun naming a particular gemstone rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Old Testament, it is associated with valuable stones used in sacred craftsmanship and ornamentation. The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Ezekiel, consistently identifying this stone. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the name of the gemstone itself.

This Hebrew word describes someone or something as “robbed”—marked by loss or deprivation. It functions as a descriptive word for a person, condition, or situation in which what was present or expected is no longer possessed. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including passages using it of people and of a barren condition. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “third,” identifying a person or thing that comes after the first and second in an ordered series. It is an ordinal expression, so it can describe position, rank, or sequence rather than naming a separate object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 108 times, appearing in descriptions of days, people, offerings, arranged groups, and other numbered sequences. Its exact force depends on what is being ordered in the surrounding passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to something “heard.” It names a message or report received through hearing, whether the matter is encouraging, alarming, or significant. In the Old Testament, it occurs 27 times, showing a broad use for what people hear and respond to. Its settings include news arriving, a reputation becoming known, and information affecting a person’s confidence or action. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of being “together,” describing things brought into a connected or entwined condition. It functions as an action word rather than naming a person or object. In the Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Job 40:17 and Lamentations 1:14. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic sense points to things gathered or held together in relation to one another.

This Hebrew word refers to “peacocks,” the distinctive birds named among the valuable goods brought into Solomon’s kingdom. It is a noun for a specific kind of bird, not a general term for birds or animals. The word appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in 1 Kings and once in 2 Chronicles, with the same rendering in both places. Its meaning is therefore narrow and concrete: peacocks as an imported or possessed item in royal wealth.
